chapter: Gangsters, records, women musicians and the blues
title: The first USO units: CBI, Three Rhythm Rascals, ETO and Eisenhower
summary: Dick Campbell sent her first to China, Burma and India with the Three Rhythm Rascals, then to Europe where she performed for Eisenhower, Zhukov and Montgomery; she earned ribbons for danger.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Now we were talking about -- we didn't get into -- you did a lot of work for the USO, In the CBI -- China, Burma --
India. Yeah. China, Burma, India. That was my first tour for USO. And Dick Campbell sent me. He was the one that -- you know, the getting together of the talent for USO, you know, the colored talent.
This was when, World War II?
Yeah, the beginning of World War II.
Well no, I was over there on Pearl Harbor. I don't know. Yeah, because I know we -- I've got pictures. Did I show you the pictures, me in Pearl Harbor?
A long time ago you showed me --

Yeah, uh-huh. Yeah. I'm trying to think, because they sent us over just after -- when the war was just declared. How did I get over there on Pearl Harbor? I guess World War II, the beginning of World War II, yes. Because --

The three -- it was my unit, because I was the manager of the unit. They made me manager of each one of my units. I was the business manager for them. I paid the salaries and everything. They'd send me the money and I'd pay them and all. Advance some money if they wanted money and all. So that was the Three Rhythm Rascals. Arlie Crawford on guitar, Al Elkins on bass, and I cannot think of Leonard's name, he was on piano. They were the musicians, the Three Rhythm Rascals. We went all through China, Burma and India. That's the first unit, Rhythm and the Blues.
The next unit, they came back, they sent me out, the ETO. That was the European Theater of Operations. Went all through France and England and Germany and all those places.

And that's when I did the command performance for General Eisenhower. They sent a plane to Nancy, France and took me to Frankfurt, Germany, to the command headquarters, where Marshall Zukov presented General Eisenhower with a medal, you know, and Field Marshall Montgomery was there. He was one of the people. And I didn't know, you know, I've always had a lot of nerve. I went up and asked all of them for their autographs. I have all their autographs. Yeah. And we played all through the European theater, and I came back. I first got a medal -- a ribbon, for ETO, because that was during all the danger, you know. Because over in India, you know, the Indians, I don't know how they would get the sound, but they would get the sound long before we would get the siren sound, and they'd start running. Well, when they'd start running, we'd start running, too, you know. We'd put our washbasins over our heads and run, which was dangerous, because if ever one of those things hit that tin washbasin, you know. So anyhow, they gave us ribbons for services, you know.

Yeah. And also the Navy. I have a thing from the Navy, too, yeah. So then after we came back from CBI we went to ETO, and that's where I said Marshall Zukov presented a medal to General Eisenhower. Then we came back
and went all through the South Pacific, all through Japan and all over the -- let me see, Korea, all up across the 38th Parallel, all up that way.
